data: Japan's first satellite Ohsumi (1970), the M-V rockets, Hayabusa and Epsilon

Launch site of Japan's scientific satellites, on the Pacific coast of Kagoshima Prefecture; it was the Kagoshima Space Center until JAXA formed in 2003. The first orbital attempt, a Lambda 4S on 26 September 1966, failed; Ohsumi reached orbit on 11 February 1970. Facts from Wikipedia (Uchinoura Space Center, Lambda, Ohsumi, M-V, Epsilon), the ISAS Ohsumi page and the JAXA site page; coordinates are the Lambda pad on Wikipedia.

Uchinoura Space Center sits on the Pacific coast of Kagoshima Prefecture, on Kyushu, in hilly ground at 31 degrees north. It opened in February 1962 as the Kagoshima Space Center and took its present name when JAXA formed in 2003. After four failed launches, a Lambda 4S-5 put Ohsumi in orbit on 11 February 1970, Japan's first satellite. Until the solid-fuel M-V rockets retired in 2006, every Japanese scientific satellite flew from here: HALCA in 1997, the Nozomi Mars probe in July 1998, Hayabusa to asteroid Itokawa on 9 May 2003, ASTRO-E2 in 2005 and Hinode on 22 September 2006. The smaller Epsilon rocket first flew from Uchinoura on 14 September 2013 with the SPRINT-A satellite. Large antennas at the site also talk to deep-space probes.
First asteroid sample ever returned to Earth (~1,500 grains of Itokawa dust, sub-milligram total)
